html:
Conversation workspaces

The desktop conversation header has Workspace | Agent views. Agent keeps the existing conversation, composer and task controls. Switching views does not stop either agent. The selected view is remembered per conversation in the browser tab. Workspace requires a Gateway advertising code_workspace_v1; older Gateways continue to support Agent mode.

You can open Workspace from a new, empty conversation before sending a message. Select an execution Gateway in Agent mode, then choose Workspace. This saves the conversation with its current settings and opens an empty project without starting a task. Any unsent Agent draft is preserved.

Workspace opens the active project on the conversation's assigned Gateway. The project selector can create a project, clone a remote repository, or explicitly connect an existing gateway folder. Each project has a server-owned identity and gateway binding. Selecting another project affects new requests; running and queued requests keep their accepted project. Changing the conversation's Gateway never moves existing source.

The compact workspace contains a standard VS Code-based file explorer, editor tabs, resizable split editors and a Code | Agent conversation sidebar. Code uses the Agent's conversation components with an independent coding thread. Agent shows the same live SRE conversation as the main Agent view, including its draft and task controls. Switching tabs starts no task and shares no chat history. The sidebar defaults to Code and remembers its selection per conversation in this browser tab.

The Agent tab hosts the complete original Agent view, including its right-side pull-out settings, Navigator, and immersive/Debug mode switch. These are the same controls and preferences as the standalone Agent view. Resizing the sidebar uses the Agent view's normal responsive layout; switching views preserves drafts, replies and running tasks.

File and editor … menus expose additional actions; the command palette (Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P) also provides Save all files, Search files, Source change history, Compare with saved file, Take over editing, Download file, and Show command output. Rename and move files using the explorer's context menu or drag and drop. The browser sees the selected project through its server-owned gateway binding. Editor code, workers, grammars, themes and third-party notices ship with the application and require no CDN.

Workspace checks the selected Gateway's current capabilities before creating its source directory. After a Gateway update, an older saved capability list does not require another installation or a manual refresh. If the Gateway is disconnected, reconnect it and try again. An upgrade message means the connected Gateway reported that Workspace support is absent.

Workspace honors the existing header pin setting. When unpinned, the header hides and frees its row; move the pointer to the top edge or focus a header control to reveal it. Pin it again to keep it visible. Switching between Agent and Workspace does not change this setting.

Editing and recovery

Direct edits autosave after a short pause. Save all and Ctrl/Cmd+S save immediately. Sending a coding prompt or an Agent request with workspace attachments saves pending edits first. The status line reports saves, disconnected storage and conflicts. Unsaved source is cached in this browser separately from chat drafts, under account, conversation and file identity. Keep this browser profile until a failed save has been reconciled.

Reloading restores the conversation's source tabs and active file within this browser tab. Retained unsaved buffers are restored separately; a changed saved revision is shown as a conflict instead of overwriting either version.

An editing reservation prevents another editor or agent from writing the same file. Two tabs also have separate reservations. Take over invalidates the previous reservation before allowing another write. Reservations expire after 30 seconds without renewal. Agent prompts release saved editor reservations so the coder can work. Agents use observed file revisions; a stale write never replaces newer source silently.

workspace.write replaces the complete file; workspace.patch applies targeted edits against an observed revision. An empty replacement of saved content is rejected unless the tool explicitly declares that emptying the file is intended. Finishing a task does not require another write. Rejected replacements preserve source and create no successful change card; direct human edits and intentional empty files remain supported.

Compare with saved file shows saved source beside a retained draft. Accepting the draft makes a new revision-checked edit. Source change history shows durable before/after diffs and offers undo. Undo fails if newer work would be overwritten. Source changed outside the application refreshes a clean buffer; dirty buffers are retained for comparison. Removed files retain any open buffer for recovery.

Directory listings and text searches use bounded pages; reads can use byte ranges. Text edits currently support files up to 32 MiB, and resumable binary uploads use chunks up to 1 MiB within the gateway transfer limit and workspace edit limit. Source snapshots currently support up to 1,000,000 entries and 8 GiB. The last 100 changes are retained for undo. Large repositories prepare asynchronously; the first copy can take substantially longer than subsequent commands. These are enforced limits, not a claim that every operation is constant-memory.

Two agents, separate histories

Code has its own history and task lane, with cancellation and recovery through the shared runtime. New Code tasks use execution profile 2 and resolve applicable settings through the parent Agent conversation: permissions, enabled skills, model routing, reasoning, budgets, Agent Checks, scheduling, terminal behavior, context, memory and redaction retain their existing owners and precedence. Disabled checks remain disabled. Code can retrieve its own older discussion without retrieving Agent chat history. Configured shared memory and knowledge remain governed by the same switches and access rules as Agent.

Code exposes a coding capability profile intersected with configured skills and permissions. Task-contract, prose, context and memory switches retain their existing settings. Code guidance asks it to inspect source, make the requested change, verify proportionately when permitted, and distinguish saved changes from execution-copy proposals.

Project rules and retained legacy context

New profile-2 tasks capture project identity, source revision, repository state and root instructions. Source reads include applicable root and nested AGENTS.md files and their revisions, with ranged retrieval for longer instructions. Context limits use the configured shared settings. Successful receipts remain available through clarification, steering and recovery.

Code can search its own earlier discussions when a follow-up needs more context, such as “use the second approach.” It retrieves retained user requests and final replies with task and workspace-result references. Individual requests can be read in pages of up to 12,000 characters. Deleted requests and other threads, accounts and SRE conversations are excluded. Historical discussions never grant permission to run commands or repeat previous edits.

Use root and nested AGENTS.md files for lasting project rules. Code creates or changes them only when requested and saves them through the same reservations, revision checks and history as other source. Current explicit instructions take precedence. Project instructions do not grant permissions or override account/gateway boundaries.

Legacy profile-1 requests retain their accepted context version, including the optional SMTO_CODE_CONTEXT_POLICY=lean_v1 behavior: one bounded recent exchange, root rules and paged older discussion. New profile-2 clients use shared context settings. Retry and restart never silently upgrade an accepted task.

Ask the coding agent to write, revise, or explain code. Agent writes update clean open editors and the file tree live. Select code and focus Describe an edit, or ask about code… to attach a removable file-and-lines reference automatically. Ask coding agent about selection also attaches it explicitly. Without a selection, the composer references the active file. Removing the reference suppresses automatic attachment for that draft. Send saves pending edits and releases clean reservations before the agent starts; save conflicts retain the unsent draft.

Code receives the file identity, saved revision and selected range without source text in its initial context. It retrieves selected code on demand through workspace.get_selection, or uses bounded workspace.read for a file reference and surrounding source. The reference stays pinned to the submitted revision across later edits, retries and task resumption. An explanation request does not ask the agent to edit files or run commands. This requires a gateway advertising code_editor_context_v1.

Code always uses the immersive layout: plain replies, a compact composer and one activity status line while work is active. There is no idle status bubble. It shows actual tool activity and saved file-change cards, followed by one final reply. Each card shows the filename, green additions and red deletions. Expand it for a unified diff, open the full editor diff, or request revision-checked undo. Counts come from committed source, not model text. Replayed events preserve the existing messages and expanded diffs. Historical diffs describe the recorded edit even if the file has since changed. Agent edits in the workspace use these same cards.

Each task summarizes its distinct changed files and committed line totals, for example 2 files changed · +1123 −2343. Multiple saved edits remain individually inspectable; editing a file twice counts it once in the file total. Open file opens its current source in the editor on the left. The native file explorer colors files with saved agent changes and includes change details in their tooltips. Its A, M and R badges yield to the lock icon when a file is read-only. These represent saved workspace changes, not Git status.

Your direct editor saves also appear in Code chat under Your saved edits, with the same green additions, red deletions and expandable historical diffs. These records appear after a successful save and stay separate from the coding agent's task totals.

Code writes and edits files by default. It runs scripts, tests, builds, benchmarks, service probes or dependency installations only when you explicitly request that action and the existing permission policy permits it. Asking Code to write a test or benchmark script does not request execution. Full Access and enabled command tools do not expand your requested scope. Existing accepted requests and older clients retain their captured command setting. Requested commands run in saved execution copies using the same authorization, executable rules, sudo handling, cancellation and receipts as Agent. These remain ordinary gateway processes, with its existing OS permissions; Code does not introduce an OS sandbox.

Use the sidebar's Agent tab to request deployment or host administration unrelated to development. Code can install development toolchains and project dependencies under the same permission and sudo policies. The active file is offered as a removable attachment chip; attach additional files from the editor with Attach active file. Changing editor tabs does not replace an attachment. Removing a suggested file suppresses it until the draft is cleared or sent. On Send, source is saved and captured as an immutable snapshot through the normal SRE task queue. Conflicts retain the draft and prevent submission. Later editing does not change that task's source, and submission retries reuse its identity and snapshot. Direct Agent requests do not automatically create Code replies. Earlier explicit handoff records remain available through the existing APIs; pending handoffs continue through their original lifecycle.

In the Agent composer, choose Special actions → Use workspace, or write @use_workspace Explain main.py. This tells the Agent to resolve file names inside this conversation's workspace using its file tools. Ambiguous names require clarification; missing files are reported rather than searched for in other conversations. Sending this shortcut saves pending source edits and releases clean editor reservations. It requests no build, edit or deployment by itself and never grants additional permissions. The choice stays with that task and its continuations, not later requests. Code already works inside the workspace and does not need the shortcut. Code and Agent histories remain independent.

To repair a script, ask Code to make it executable and run it. Code can save POSIX permissions using workspace.chmod, including metadata-only changes such as 0600 → 0700, and verify ./hello.sh in an execution copy. Permission changes appear in history without fabricated line additions and survive reload and undo. workspace.stat supplies a state revision even when file contents are unreadable. Agent can use @use_workspace Run script.sh or an attached workspace file, subject to its existing policies.

Terminal

Select Terminal at the bottom right of the editor, or choose Open terminal from an editor … menu or the command palette. The standard terminal panel opens below the editor. Drag its top edge to resize it; hide the panel to reclaim editor space. Hiding it or switching Workspace/Agent views preserves the shell and its running commands. Use the terminal's trash action to end a session.

The shell runs on the conversation's assigned Gateway and starts in its workspace folder. For example, enter python3 script.py or sh script.sh to run a saved file. It supports ordinary shell input, command history, Ctrl+C and interactive program prompts. Enter and pasted commands save pending editor buffers first. A save failure or conflict prevents that input from being sent; resolve the conflict or use Ctrl+C to clear the pending shell command.

Manual terminal commands operate directly in the workspace with the Gateway's existing OS permissions. They can change the source files; external changes refresh clean editors and preserve conflicting unsaved buffers. The coding agent's build/test commands continue to use saved execution copies under the shared command policy. Opening a terminal does not enable agent command tools or submit an agent task.

The terminal uses VS Code colors that follow the app's light/dark theme, including readable ANSI output, cursor and selection highlights. New User, Agent and Code shells show colored directories and prompt markers; commands keep their own output colors. Set NO_COLOR in the gateway environment or shell startup file before opening a new shell to keep its prompt plain. Theme changes preserve existing output and running sessions.

Output reconnects with a cursor, and repeated input receipts do not execute a command twice. A gateway restart or expired session requires a new terminal; commands are not replayed into a new shell. Up to four sessions are available per workspace, with bounded recent output. Interactive terminals currently require an updated Linux/macOS Gateway; Windows Gateways retain the existing command-output and build/test flow.

To investigate an error, select the terminal containing it and tell Code “check the terminal and fix the script”, type @check_terminal, or use Check terminal beside the Code composer. Code can read recent commands and errors from the selected User, Code or Agent terminal in this project. The selection is captured when you send the request; changing tabs later does not redirect that task. The shortcut inserts text into your draft; sending the request asks Code to inspect it.

Terminal context is a read-only view of retained output. It does not rerun the command or type into the shell. Code inspects the current source, saves requested fixes, and verifies them in a saved execution copy under your existing settings. Say “diagnose only; do not edit or run” for inspection only. Recent output is bounded and reports truncation; plain User terminals cannot supply per-command exit codes. An updated gateway advertising code_terminal_context_v1 is required. External desktop terminals, expired sessions and output lost on gateway restart are unavailable; paste the error in those cases. Reading an empty terminal cannot recover earlier output.

Run agent commands in the terminal panel

In the Agent conversation's view settings, enable Run in workspace terminal to attach the Agent and Code tabs. The choice is saved for that conversation and defaults to off. Activation requires an initialized workspace and an updated POSIX Gateway configured for Bash 5 or newer. Controller, Gateway and UI must support the shared-shell protocol together.

Switching the conversation between Agent and Code selects its matching terminal, including after reload or after using a User terminal. Existing output and running processes are preserved, and keyboard focus stays in the conversation. A closed managed view is reattached when terminals are enabled. Switching conversation tabs does not enable the terminal setting.

Agent and Code are persistent shared shells: type your own commands when a tab is idle. Ordinary cd and export changes carry forward between you and that tab's agent. Each tab runs one foreground command at a time. The agent waits while you compose a command or while your command runs. Agent, Code and User remain independent. Commands with supplied stdin, Python actions, explicit BatchModeNoTTY, and managed elevation retain their existing execution mode. Explicit working directories and saved execution copies are preserved. Code follows the same effective settings as Agent.

Agent commands display ordinary Git logs, diffs and other paged output directly. These pager defaults apply only to the agent command; your shell's pager settings remain intact. An explicitly selected pager still accepts interactive input and participates in the normal handoff, including when its prompt follows a wrapped line.

The tabs show the current command, directory and state. During interactive execution, typing answers the running program; it does not start another shell command. These answers do not trigger editor saves. Select Terminal to open your independent User shell, or New user terminal for an additional shell, even while agent commands run. Use Ctrl+C or existing Stop controls to cancel work; closing a managed tab only detaches its view. Choose Show Agent and Code terminals from the editor menu or command palette to reattach.

Reset, beside the Output and Terminal panel tabs, restores a usable panel height after resizing or maximizing. It preserves terminal sessions and their output.

When an agent-started command requests input, the terminal status and task activity show Your turn — agent takes over in 10s. Silence alone does not start a timer. Typing pauses handoff until you submit. Let agent handle skips the countdown and clears unfinished input without submitting it when the program provides a safe line-clearing boundary. Otherwise control stays with you. At expiry the agent inspects the output and answers using the task context; processing may take additional time. Missing answers or credentials show Your answer is needed. Commands you start never receive automatic takeover.

Change Workspace terminal input timeout (seconds) in Settings → Execution. It accepts positive whole seconds, defaults to 10, and applies to the next input request. Each new prompt has its own countdown; refreshing the same prompt does not restart it. Task Pause freezes the countdown and Stop cancels it.

Hiding the workspace or disconnecting the browser does not stop execution. Reloading restores the same countdown or typing pause and replays bounded recent output. Session loss never replays commands. Turning the setting off immediately disables pending takeover and changes subsequent agent commands to their original execution flow; already-running commands continue. If a saved-on setting becomes unavailable, execution reports the problem instead of silently using a different route.

Lifecycle

Creating a conversation does not create source folders. Opening Workspace provisions private project metadata in the gateway account namespace. New and cloned projects use owned source storage; connected folders remain externally owned. Disconnecting a project, deleting a conversation or retiring workspace storage never deletes an externally owned folder. Reconnect restores a disconnected project identity after checking its root.

Automatic conversation purge preserves conversations with workspaces. Ordinary task cleanup preserves source and change history. Explicit conversation deletion uses the existing review and confirmation behavior for owned source, execution copies and coding history. It fences new work and waits for active operations to settle. Disconnected gateways leave cleanup pending until they reconnect.

Explicit workspace deletion closes terminal sessions before cleanup. Linux is the qualification target for this implementation. Existing macOS/Windows paths remain compatible where their advertised capabilities support an operation; full qualification on those platforms is not claimed. Graphical debugger integration, extension marketplaces and mobile editing are outside this scope.

Execution sessions and repository operations

Related commands reuse an execution session with a recorded source baseline. Existing repositories use managed detached Git worktrees; other projects use incremental copies. Dependencies are retained while interpreter and dependency fingerprints match. Outstanding execution edits must be reconciled before refreshing saved source. Inspect workspace.execution_changes, then import explicit source paths. Build products, caches and .git must not be imported as ordinary source. A successful command alone does not establish that its changes were saved. Conflicts retain the execution proposal and protect newer source.

Code can use configured Shell, Python, file, Git/GitHub, documentation, web/browser, development container/database and artifact tools. Tool selection is intersected with the coding role and existing policy. Infrastructure administration, deployments and unrelated communications remain in Agent. Missing tools report the concrete policy, gateway, software, authentication or project prerequisite. Browser verification and existing authenticated artifact previews use the gateway's advertised browser/artifact facilities.

Configured scheduling is available in Code. A scheduled coding task stays in its Code discussion and retains the selected project even if another project becomes active. Each occurrence revalidates project ownership and captures its source context. It follows the existing scheduling, model and permission settings.

workspace.git targets the canonical selected repository and reserves it against concurrent editor mutations. It supports ordinary Git commands under the shared Shell policy. Commits select explicit paths and preserve unrelated staged work; including existing staged changes requires that scope in the request. Commit, push, PR and CI mutations require the user's requested scope and existing policy. After an uncertain remote outcome, inspect refs or provider state before retrying.

Repository symlinks are preserved as entries; project file operations do not follow them outside authorized roots. Execution processes retain ordinary gateway filesystem access. Binary assets can be read in ranges and uploaded in resumable chunks. Content hashes remain available alongside opaque metadata state revisions. Legacy snapshots without a metadata baseline require a fresh snapshot before metadata import.

Activity and connection failures

Code uses the shared task lifecycle for active, waiting, paused, blocked and terminal states. Completed trace streams send an explicit completion event, close, and reconnect only for live work. Reconnection resumes using event cursors and trace generation identity.

Transport errors retain a sanitized endpoint, method, time, exception category and available request/task/server correlation IDs. Transport failures use browser_transport; HTTP errors retain their server stage. Abort is distinct from failure. A lost mutation response is an uncertain result: reconcile its retained submission or operation identity before retrying. Drafts and source buffers remain available for recovery.

Linux qualification

The implementation's recorded qualification status is in docs/code-mode-linux-v2-qualification.json. Test receipts, model transcripts, package checks and performance measurements are retained locally under artifacts/code-mode-v2/. A passing isolated fixture does not qualify a remote provider account or authorize publishing to it. Remote GitHub qualification requires an approved disposable repository; release remains gated on the recorded outstanding items.

The 100,009-entry qualification fixture contains 76,296,726 source bytes. In the measured run, asynchronous preparation acknowledged in 2 ms and a concurrent directory read took 11 ms. Cold preparation took 130 seconds, reuse took 12 seconds, and peak process RSS was approximately 566 MiB. These are local measurements, not guaranteed latency or memory bounds on other hosts. Existing resource budgets and advertised source limits still apply.
